qs.q: An infant presents with microcephaly, hearing loss, and imaging findings showing periventricular intracranial calcifications. Which congenital pathogen is most strongly implicated in this clinical picture?
qs.e: Congenital cytomegalovirus infection typically causes hearing loss, microcephaly, and periventricular calcifications. Toxoplasmosis tends to produce intracranial calcifications distributed more diffusely rather than specifically periventricular.
qs.s: Neonatology 6: Congenital Conditions, Emergencies and Follow-up: MCQs

qs.q: A 20-year-old male with sensorineural hearing loss and progressive renal failure develops anterior lenticonus. This ocular lesion is a direct consequence of a structural defect in which component?
o: Immunoglobulin deposition within the anterior chamber angle
Fibrillin microfibrils supporting the suspensory lens ligaments
Type II collagen within the primary vitreous humor matrix
Type IV collagen within the lens capsule basement membrane
qs.e: Anterior lenticonus in Alport syndrome results from structural defects in the basement membrane of the lens capsule, which is rich in type IV collagen alpha chains. Fibrillin defects are associated with Marfan syndrome rather than Alport syndrome.

qs.q: A neonate is evaluated for congenital anomalies and is found to have sensorineural hearing loss, microcephaly, and periventricular calcifications. A urine PCR confirms a viral infection that is a member of the TORCH group. Which cytopathological feature is classically associated with this virus?
o: Koplik spots on the buccal mucosa
qs.e: Cytomegalovirus characteristically forms 'owl's eye' intranuclear inclusion bodies in infected cells. Negri bodies are instead associated with rabies virus infection.

ai.title: Pediatric Hearing Loss
ai.subject: Paediatrics
ai.summary: Hearing loss in children is a common sensory disorder that can impair language development and academic performance. In low‑resource settings, recurrent otitis media with effusion is the leading cause, but congenital and acquired factors must also be considered.

sections.p: Hearing loss is a reduction in the ability to detect sound across frequencies, classified as conductive, sensorineural, or mixed. Diagnosis relies on age‑appropriate history, otoscopic examination, and audiometry when available.
b: Conductive loss: problem in outer or middle ear, improves with bone conduction.
Sensorineural loss: inner ear or auditory nerve pathology, bone and air conduction both reduced.
Mixed loss: features of both.

sections.p: Severity is graded by pure‑tone average (PTA) in the better ear, when audiometry can be performed. In low‑resource settings, behavioral audiometry or the Whisper Test can approximate severity.
b: Mild: PTA 26‑40 dB – difficulty hearing soft speech.
Moderate: PTA 41‑55 dB – need louder speech, may miss classroom instruction.
Moderately‑severe: PTA 56‑70 dB – requires amplification for most communication.
Severe: PTA 71‑90 dB – only loud sounds heard, speech perception poor.
Profound: PTA >90 dB – little or no functional hearing.

sections.p: Causes are grouped by site of lesion and by epidemiology in East African settings.
b: Conductive: Recurrent otitis media with effusion (most common), chronic suppurative otitis media, tympanic membrane perforation, foreign body.
Sensorineural: Congenital cytomegalovirus, meningitis, neonatal hypoxia, ototoxic drugs (e.g., aminoglycosides, cisplatin), malaria‑related cerebral involvement, HIV‑related neuropathy.
Mixed: Chronic middle‑ear disease with inner‑ear damage, severe malaria with both middle‑ear effusion and inner‑ear toxicity.

sections.p: Children may not verbalise loss; look for language delay, poor speech articulation, inattentiveness, and social withdrawal.
b: Delayed babbling or speech milestones.
Failure to respond to name or loud sounds.
Frequent requests to repeat information.
Ear rubbing, clumsiness, or balance problems (if vestibular involvement).

sections.p: Select tests that answer specific clinical questions; adapt when equipment is lacking.

t.b: Is there middle‑ear pathology? – Finds effusion, perforation, or foreign body; guides immediate treatment.
Is the middle ear pressure abnormal? – Type B curve suggests effusion; Type C suggests eustachian tube dysfunction.
What is the functional hearing level? – Determines severity; if unavailable, use parental report and speech‑language assessment.
Is outer‑hair‑cell function intact? – Absent OAEs indicate sensorineural loss; useful in newborn screening.
Is an infectious cause present? – Positive CMV IgM suggests congenital infection; HIV guides antiretroviral therapy.

t.a: Imaging (CT temporal bone or MRI) – if referral possible
t.b: Is there structural abnormality? – Detects cholesteatoma, inner‑ear malformations; otherwise refer to tertiary centre.

sections.p: Identify children at risk of irreversible loss or systemic disease.
b: Persistent otorrhea >2 weeks despite antibiotics.
Sudden unilateral loss.
Associated fever, meningismus, or neurologic deficit.
Failure to achieve speech milestones by 12 months.
Signs of systemic infection (e.g., HIV, TB).

sections.p: Treat the underlying cause first, then address hearing rehabilitation.
b: Acute otitis media with effusion: nasal saline, decongestants, short‑course oral antibiotics if bacterial infection suspected.
Chronic suppurative otitis media: topical antibiotic ear drops, ear cleaning, possible myringotomy.
Ototoxic drug avoidance: stop aminoglycosides or cisplatin when feasible; substitute with less ototoxic agents.
Hearing amplification: low‑cost bone‑conduction devices or behind‑the‑ear hearing aids; fit after audiometry.
Speech‑language therapy: early referral to therapist to prevent language delay.
Vaccination: pneumococcal and Haemophilus influenzae type b vaccines to reduce middle‑ear infections.

sections.p: Regular monitoring ensures timely intervention and tracks progression.
b: Re‑evaluate hearing every 6 months in children with chronic middle‑ear disease.
Educate caregivers on ear hygiene and avoiding insertion of objects.
Promote exclusive breastfeeding and nutrition to support immune function.
Implement school‑based hearing screening programs.

sections.p: Conditions that mimic hearing loss but have different pathophysiology.
b: Auditory processing disorder – normal audiogram but difficulty interpreting sounds.
Speech‑language disorder – language deficits without true auditory deficit.
Vertigo or vestibular dysfunction – balance symptoms without hearing loss.
Normal tympanogram in early effusion – may be missed without careful otoscopy.
Absent OAEs in noisy environment – false‑positive sensorineural loss.
Parent‑reported hearing may underestimate mild loss.

faq.q: Why is otitis media with effusion the leading cause of hearing loss in this region?
faq.a: Frequent upper‑respiratory infections, crowded living conditions, and limited access to timely antibiotics impair eustachian tube function, leading to fluid accumulation.

faq.q: Can hearing improve after treating chronic otitis media?
faq.a: Yes, removal of middle‑ear effusion and infection often restores conductive hearing; persistent loss may need amplification.

faq.q: When should a child be referred for specialist audiology?
faq.a: If hearing loss is moderate or greater, if language delay persists after infection treatment, or if there are red‑flag symptoms.

exam: A 3‑year‑old with recurrent ear discharge presents with speech delay – what is your next step? — Perform otoscopic exam, assess for effusion, and start appropriate topical antibiotics; arrange audiometry.

How does conductive hearing loss differ from sensorineural loss on tuning‑fork tests? — Conductive loss shows louder bone‑conduction (Weber to affected ear), sensorineural loss shows louder air‑conduction (Weber to normal ear).

A child on cisplatin chemotherapy develops high‑frequency hearing loss – which drug class is responsible and what alternative could be considered? — Platinum agents cause ototoxicity; consider non‑platinum regimens if oncologically appropriate.
What red‑flag symptom would prompt urgent referral for possible central cause? — Sudden unilateral loss with neurologic signs (e.g., facial palsy, seizures).
Explain why the Whisper test is useful in a rural clinic. — It requires no equipment, assesses functional hearing, and helps grade severity for referral.
A child with HIV presents with chronic otitis media – how does HIV alter management? — Higher risk of atypical pathogens; use broader‑spectrum topical antibiotics and monitor for systemic infection.
Why is early speech‑language therapy critical after treating otitis media with effusion? — Prevents irreversible language delay and supports academic development.
What vaccination strategy reduces the incidence of pediatric hearing loss in low‑resource settings? — Routine pneumococcal and Hib vaccination lowers middle‑ear infection rates.
